problem: The lead says a cell sits at 'every chip pin', but Section 1 says 'every digital I/O pin'. Boundary-scan cells cover digital pins only; analog, supply and clock pins are not in the BSR. A student may think every pin on the package is included.
fix: Say consistently: 'A boundary-scan cell sits at every digital input, output and bidirectional pin. Analog and supply pins are outside the boundary scan register.'

problem: 'Inside are four registers' lists IDCODE as one of them, but IDCODE is optional in IEEE 1149.1 and the next paragraph correctly says 'most devices also provide IDCODE'. A device without it has only three of these registers.
fix: Say: 'Three registers are always present: the instruction register, the 1-bit bypass register and the boundary scan register. Most devices add a fourth, the optional IDCODE register.'

problem: The text gives the sampling edge for TMS only. Students often assume TDI is sampled on the same edge that TDO changes on, which is wrong and causes timing mistakes when they read a TAP timing diagram.
fix: Add: 'TDI and TMS are sampled on the rising edge of TCK; TDO changes on the falling edge of TCK.'

problem: The answer says an open trace 'can hold the net at 0'. With the driver sending 1 and the trace open, the receiving cell input floats, so the captured bit is not reliable — it may read 0, read 1, or keep the last value. Only the short to ground gives a dependable 0.
fix: Answer: 'A short of the net to ground gives a solid 0; an open trace leaves the receiving pin floating, so it may also capture 0 instead of the driven 1. The instruction in use is EXTEST.'
